blocks.text: 29.3 Auto Pan-Tremolo
blocks.raw_html: 29.3 Auto Pan-Tremolo

blocks.text: Auto Pan-Tremolo uses LFO modulation to affect the input signal’s stereo position or amplitude to create automatic panning, tremolo, and gating effects.
blocks.raw_html: Auto Pan-Tremolo uses LFO modulation to affect the input signal’s stereo position or amplitude to create automatic panning, tremolo, and gating effects.

blocks.text: There are two modes available: Panning and Tremolo. In Panning mode, two LFOs modulate the placement of the input signal within the stereo panorama by alternating its amplitude between the left and right channels. In Tremolo mode, a single LFO modulates the signal’s amplitude to create variation in volume. Use the respective toggles to switch between modes. The LFO waveform and controls in the display update depending on which mode is selected to reflect its corresponding properties.
blocks.raw_html: There are two modes available: Panning and Tremolo. In Panning mode, two LFOs modulate the placement of the input signal within the stereo panorama by alternating its amplitude between the left and right channels. In Tremolo mode, a single LFO modulates the signal’s amplitude to create variation in volume. Use the respective toggles to switch between modes. The LFO waveform and controls in the display update depending on which mode is selected to reflect its corresponding properties.

blocks.text: The real-time visualization below the LFO waveform shows the current stereo position in Panning mode or the current amplitude level in Tremolo mode. This makes it easy to see at a glance how the input signal is moving across the left and right channels or how its amplitude is fluctuating.

This makes it easy to see at a glance how the input signal is moving across the left and right channels or how its amplitude is fluctuating.

blocks.text: Use the Waveform drop-down to select an LFO shape: Sine, Triangle, Shark Tooth, Saw Up, Saw Down, Square, Random, Wander, and S&H (Sample and Hold).
blocks.raw_html: Use the Waveform drop-down to select an LFO shape: Sine, Triangle, Shark Tooth, Saw Up, Saw Down, Square, Random, Wander, and S&H (Sample and Hold).

blocks.text: Select one of the available Time modes to determine the rate of the LFO: Rate, Time, Synced, Dotted, Triplet, or 16th. Once selected, the corresponding modulation rate control below the drop-down updates to reflect the value associated with that mode. For example, in Time mode, you can set the period of the LFO anywhere from 100 milliseconds to 200 seconds, which is useful for creating long modulation cycles.

Once selected, the corresponding modulation rate control below the drop-down updates to reflect the value associated with that mode. For example, in Time mode, you can set the period of the LFO anywhere from 100 milliseconds to 200 seconds, which is useful for creating long modulation cycles.

blocks.text: You can choose between two Stereo Offset modes: Phase and Spin. In Phase mode, the LFO waveforms for the left and right channels can be offset by a set number of degrees. At 180°, the LFOs are perfectly out of phase so that when one LFO reaches its peak value, the other is at its minimum. In Spin mode, the left and right channels diverge progressively based on the set percentage. This adds a subtle asymmetry between the two channels. Note that only Phase mode is available when using the Random, Wander, and S&H waveforms.

At 180°, the LFOs are perfectly out of phase so that when one LFO reaches its peak value, the other is at its minimum. In Spin mode, the left and right channels diverge progressively based on the set percentage. This adds a subtle asymmetry between the two channels. Note that only Phase mode is available when using the Random, Wander, and S&H waveforms.

blocks.text: When using any of the beat-division-based Time modes (Synced, Triplet, Dotted, or 16th), the Phase Offset control becomes available and can be used to shift the starting point of each LFO channel within its cycle relative to the beat grid. This is useful for offsetting the modulation so that it begins slightly before or after the beat.

This is useful for offsetting the modulation so that it begins slightly before or after the beat.

blocks.text: When using the Random, Wander, or S&H waveforms, Phase Offset functions as a stereo width control and can be used to introduce variation between the channels.
blocks.raw_html: When using the Random, Wander, or S&H waveforms, Phase Offset functions as a stereo width control and can be used to introduce variation between the channels.

blocks.text: Use the Invert toggle to flip the polarity of the LFO. When enabled, the positive and negative values of the waveform are swapped, which effectively turns the waveform upside down. In Panning mode, for example, inverting the Saw Up waveform creates a Saw Down waveform. In Tremolo mode, the peaks of the waveform become the valleys and vice versa. When using ramp-shaped waveforms, enabling Invert produces a ducking effect, while disabling it creates a gating effect.

blocks.text: Tremolo mode includes two additional options that can be enabled to influence the behavior of the LFO modulation: Harmonic and Vintage.
blocks.raw_html: Tremolo mode includes two additional options that can be enabled to influence the behavior of the LFO modulation: Harmonic and Vintage.

blocks.text: With Harmonic enabled, the high and low frequencies are modulated in an alternating pattern rather than in parallel. A fixed crossover of 600 Hz splits the signal into two frequency bands.
blocks.raw_html: With Harmonic enabled, the high and low frequencies are modulated in an alternating pattern rather than in parallel. A fixed crossover of 600 Hz splits the signal into two frequency bands.

blocks.text: With Vintage enabled, the signal’s amplitude is modulated by the LFO as well as shaped by a non-linear curve, which adds warmth and grit to the tremolo effect.
blocks.raw_html: With Vintage enabled, the signal’s amplitude is modulated by the LFO as well as shaped by a non-linear curve, which adds warmth and grit to the tremolo effect.

blocks.text: Below the display are controls for adjusting the LFO’s amount, rate, shape, attack, and response to the input signal’s level.
blocks.raw_html: Below the display are controls for adjusting the LFO’s amount, rate, shape, attack, and response to the input signal’s level.

blocks.text: Use the Amount control to set how much LFO modulation is applied to the incoming signal.
blocks.raw_html: Use the Amount control to set how much LFO modulation is applied to the incoming signal.

blocks.text: The LFO rate can be set using the control to the right of the Amount control. The name and unit of this control change depending on the selected Time mode. For example, the control appears as Freq when Rate is selected and the value is set in hertz (Hz). In Time mode, the control appears as Time and the value is set in milliseconds (ms). In the Synced, Triplet, Dotted, and 16th modes, the control appears as Rate and the value is set in beat divisions.

blocks.text: Note that the values for the Amount control and the LFO rate are shared between the Panning and Tremolo modes and cannot be set independently.
blocks.raw_html: Note that the values for the Amount control and the LFO rate are shared between the Panning and Tremolo modes and cannot be set independently.

blocks.text: The Shape control affects the LFO waveform differently in each mode. In Panning mode, positive Shape values push each waveform toward its upper and lower limits. This shortens the overlap between the LFOs so that the transition from one channel to the next happens more abruptly. In Tremolo mode, positive values gradually expand the waveform to create rounded peaks, while negative values gradually compress the peaks into an angular shape. At its maximum and minimum values, the Shape control can create ramps for gating effects (with Invert off) and pumping effects (with Invert on).

blocks.text: The Attack Time slider sets how long it takes, in milliseconds, to reach the maximum amount of modulation after a transient is detected. A long attack time can be useful for applying the effect only during the sustained portion of the signal while leaving the initial peaks unaffected. In Panning mode, this keeps transients centered in the stereo field, while in Tremolo mode, this helps preserve their impact.

blocks.text: The Dynamic Frequency Modulation slider determines how much the input signal’s level affects the LFO rate. At positive values, louder signals increase the LFO rate, while negative values decrease it.

blocks.text: 29.4 Auto Shift
blocks.raw_html: 29.4 Auto Shift

blocks.text: Auto Shift is a real-time pitch tracking and correction device with controls for vibrato, pitch shifting, and formant shifting. Its design makes it especially well-suited for transforming vocals, though it can be used with any monophonic audio signal. You can pitch correct audio using a defined scale or using the MIDI notes from a separate track. Auto Shift also includes a built-in LFO, so you can modulate incoming audio over time.
blocks.raw_html: Auto Shift is a real-time pitch tracking and correction device with controls for vibrato, pitch shifting, and formant shifting. Its design makes it especially well-suited for transforming vocals, though it can be used with any monophonic audio signal. You can pitch correct audio using a defined scale or using the MIDI notes from a separate track. Auto Shift also includes a built-in LFO, so you can modulate incoming audio over time.

blocks.text: 29.4.1 Input Section
blocks.raw_html: 29.4.1 Input Section

blocks.text: Auto Shift can receive audio as well as MIDI input. The Input section lets you configure how incoming signals are processed in the device.
blocks.raw_html: Auto Shift can receive audio as well as MIDI input. The Input section lets you configure how incoming signals are processed in the device.

blocks.text: The Input Pitch display shows the pitch of the incoming audio in notes and cents.
blocks.raw_html: The Input Pitch display shows the pitch of the incoming audio in notes and cents.

blocks.text: You can set the frequency range for the audio input using one of the three Pitch Range toggles. This helps optimize the quality of the pitch estimation and correction. Use High for signals in a high frequency range, Mid for signals in a mid frequency range, and Bass for signals in a low frequency range. Each toggle has an LED that flashes when the incoming audio falls within its corresponding range.

Use High for signals in a high frequency range, Mid for signals in a mid frequency range, and Bass for signals in a low frequency range. Each toggle has an LED that flashes when the incoming audio falls within its corresponding range.

blocks.text: Note that each pitch range setting affects the device’s latency differently, so switching between toggles changes the overall latency.
blocks.raw_html: Note that each pitch range setting affects the device’s latency differently, so switching between toggles changes the overall latency.

blocks.text: You can use the Input Gain slider to adjust the gain of the incoming signal from -24 to +24 dB.
blocks.raw_html: You can use the Input Gain slider to adjust the gain of the incoming signal from -24 to +24 dB.

blocks.text: The Latency Readout displays the device’s latency in milliseconds. Enabling Live Mode via the toggle in the device’s title bar can help reduce latency, which is particularly useful for live performances. However, slight glitches may occur during note onsets or rapid pitch changes in this mode.

blocks.text: 29.4.1.1 MIDI Input
blocks.raw_html: 29.4.1.1 MIDI Input

blocks.text: Enabling MIDI input lets you use the notes from a separate MIDI track to pitch correct the incoming audio instead of tuning it to a defined scale via the Quantizer.
blocks.raw_html: Enabling MIDI input lets you use the notes from a separate MIDI track to pitch correct the incoming audio instead of tuning it to a defined scale via the Quantizer.

blocks.text: The MIDI In toggle shows or hides the MIDI Input panel, which contains track routing and voice mode settings.
blocks.raw_html: The MIDI In toggle shows or hides the MIDI Input panel, which contains track routing and voice mode settings.

blocks.text: Use the MIDI On toggle to activate or deactivate MIDI input. When enabled, the Quantizer tab is replaced with the MIDI tab, where you can further shape the behavior of incoming MIDI notes.

blocks.text: The External Source chooser sets the MIDI sidechain source, i.e., the track used to send notes to Auto Shift. The Tapping Point chooser lets you specify whether the MIDI sidechain is sent before or after any MIDI effects that are in the source track’s device chain. Select Pre FX to bypass the effects on the track, or select Post FX or Post Mixer to include them.

blocks.text: There are two voice mode toggles to choose from: Mono and Poly. Mono uses a single voice, meaning that only one note can be used for the pitch correction at a time. You can use the Glide slider to set the time that overlapping notes take to slide their pitch to the next incoming pitch. Poly can use up to eight voices at once, making it ideal for harmonization. Use the Voice Count chooser to set the maximum number of voices to 2, 4, or 8.

blocks.text: 29.4.2 Quantizer Tab
blocks.raw_html: 29.4.2 Quantizer Tab

blocks.text: The Quantizer corrects incoming audio according to the notes of a defined scale. In the Quantizer tab, you can access controls for monitoring how the signal is processed, as well as controls for adjusting the correction.
blocks.raw_html: The Quantizer corrects incoming audio according to the notes of a defined scale. In the Quantizer tab, you can access controls for monitoring how the signal is processed, as well as controls for adjusting the correction.

blocks.text: The Pitch Correction Meter displays how much the incoming signal is being shifted in cents to match the target note, which is shown beneath the meter. The target note is determined by the set scale.
blocks.raw_html: The Pitch Correction Meter displays how much the incoming signal is being shifted in cents to match the target note, which is shown beneath the meter. The target note is determined by the set scale.

blocks.text: You can adjust the intensity of the pitch correction using the Correction Strength slider. The higher the value, the more the audio is shifted to match the target note. Use the Smooth toggle to switch smoothing on or off. When enabled, pitch transitions between notes are smoothed, and more natural vibrato is retained. You can set the smoothing time from 0 to 200 milliseconds using the Smoothing Time slider. The Correction Strength and Smoothing parameters determine the overall style of the pitch correction. With these settings, you can produce results ranging from subtle and nuanced to rigid and quantized.

blocks.text: The Included Notes in Scale display determines which notes are used for the pitch correction. You can create a custom scale by selecting notes in the display, or you can set the key and scale using the Root and Scale choosers. The Pitch Shift slider can be used to transpose the pitch up or down in scale degrees; the pitch shift is applied after the correction.

Additionally, the Included Keys in Scale display highlights the selected scale’s notes in purple, and the Root and Scale choosers are deactivated.

blocks.raw_html: 29.4.3 MIDI Tab

blocks.text: The piano visualization displays notes as they are received from the source track. These notes are then used to correct the incoming audio.

blocks.text: Note that scale awareness is not available when using MIDI input. To use the notes within a specific scale, you can add the Scale MIDI effect to the source track. Make sure Auto Shift’s Tapping Point chooser is set to Post FX or Post Mixer so that the effect is included.

blocks.text: The Attack Time slider sets the attack time of the note’s envelope from 0 to 1,000 milliseconds. The Release Time slider sets the release time of the note’s envelope from 0 to 5 seconds.

blocks.text: When the Note Latch toggle is switched on, MIDI notes are held until the next Note On message. The Pitch Bend Range control sets the device’s pitch bend range, from 0 to 48 semitones.

blocks.text: In the Mod Routing section, four parameters can be modulated using MIDI or MPE data: Pitch, Formant, Volume, and Pan. Each parameter can be modulated by one of six modulation sources: Velocity, Pressure, Mod Wheel, Pitch Bend, Note PB, or Slide. Use each target’s dedicated Mod Source drop-down menu to select a modulation source, and adjust the modulation depth with its corresponding Mod Depth slider.

blocks.text: 29.4.4 LFO Tab
blocks.raw_html: 29.4.4 LFO Tab

blocks.text: You can use the built-in LFO to apply modulation to the incoming audio’s pitch, formants, volume, and panning.
blocks.raw_html: You can use the built-in LFO to apply modulation to the incoming audio’s pitch, formants, volume, and panning.

blocks.text: The LFO Reset toggle switches LFO re-triggering on or off. When enabled, the LFO’s phase will be re-triggered at note onsets. When using the Quantizer, an onset occurs when a pitch is detected after a period of unpitched audio. The Onset Indicator LED flashes when the LFO’s phase is re-triggered. With MIDI input, an onset occurs at the start of a new note, and the Onset Indicator becomes the Trigger Indicator.

blocks.text: The LFO Delay slider sets the delay time before the attack phase begins, from 0 to 1.5 seconds. The LFO Attack slider sets the attack time during which the LFO’s level increases to its peak level, from 0 to 2 seconds. As you modify either value, the waveform in the display will reflect the changes.

blocks.text: 29.4.5 Pitch Section
blocks.raw_html: 29.4.5 Pitch Section

blocks.text: You can apply both pitch and formant shifting to incoming signals using the controls in the Pitch section.
blocks.raw_html: You can apply both pitch and formant shifting to incoming signals using the controls in the Pitch section.

blocks.text: The Pitch Shift control sets the amount of transposition applied in semitones. You can use the Pitch Shift Fine slider to set the transposition in cents.

blocks.text: Use the Formant Shift control to shift the formants — the resonant frequencies that help define the tonal characteristics of a sound — within a range of -100% to 100%. At higher values, pitches will sound higher and more resonant, while at lower values pitches will sound lower and less full. Shifting formants lets you create a higher or lower sound without actually transposing the pitch.

blocks.text: 29.4.6 Vibrato Section
blocks.raw_html: 29.4.6 Vibrato Section

blocks.text: The Vibrato section contains controls for applying vibrato to incoming audio and adjusting the overall balance of the dry and processed signal.

blocks.text: There are three main vibrato controls:

blocks.text: Vibrato Amount — adjusts the depth of the vibrato, from 0 to 200 cents.

blocks.text: Vibrato Rate — adjusts the speed of the vibrato, from 2 to 15 Hz.

blocks.text: Enabling the Natural Vibrato toggle creates variations in the vibrato’s speed and depth, producing a more realistic effect.

blocks.text: The Dry/Wet slider sets the balance between the dry and processed signals. At 0%, no pitch correction is applied, while at 100%, only the pitch corrected signal is heard. You can create a doubler effect by setting this value to 50%, which equally balances the original and corrected signals.

blocks.text: 29.5 Beat Repeat
blocks.raw_html: 29.5 Beat Repeat

blocks.text: Beat Repeat allows for the creation of controlled or randomized repetitions of an incoming signal.
blocks.raw_html: Beat Repeat allows for the creation of controlled or randomized repetitions of an incoming signal.

blocks.text: The Interval control defines how often Beat Repeat captures new material and begins repeating it. Interval is synced to and set in terms of the song tempo, with values ranging from ”1/32” to ”4 Bars.” The Offset control shifts the point defined by Interval forward in time. If Interval is set to ”1 Bar,” for example, and Offset to ”8/16”, material will be captured for repetition once per bar on the third beat (i.e., halfway, or eight-sixteenths of the way, through the bar).
blocks.raw_html: The Interval control defines how often Beat Repeat captures new material and begins repeating it. Interval is synced to and set in terms of the song tempo, with values ranging from ”1/32” to ”4 Bars.” The Offset control shifts the point defined by Interval forward in time. If Interval is set to ”1 Bar,” for example, and Offset to ”8/16”, material will be captured for repetition once per bar on the third beat (i.e., halfway, or eight-sixteenths of the way, through the bar).

blocks.text: You can add randomness to the process using the Chance control, which defines the likelihood of repetitions actually taking place when Interval and Offset ”ask” for them. If Chance is set to 100 percent, repetitions will always take place at the given Interval/Offset time; if set to zero, there will be no repetitions.

If Chance is set to 100 percent, repetitions will always take place at the given Interval/Offset time; if set to zero, there will be no repetitions.

blocks.text: Gate defines the total length of all repetitions in sixteenth notes. If Gate is set to ”4/16”, the repetitions will occur over the period of one beat, starting at the position defined by Interval and Offset.

blocks.text: Activating the Repeat button bypasses all of the above controls, immediately capturing material and repeating it until deactivated.
blocks.raw_html: Activating the Repeat button bypasses all of the above controls, immediately capturing material and repeating it until deactivated.

blocks.text: The Grid control defines the grid size — the size of each repeated slice. If set to ”1/16”, a slice the size of one sixteenth note will be captured and repeated for the given Gate length (or until Repeat is deactivated). Large grid values create rhythmic loops, while small values create sonic artifacts. The No Triplets button sets grid division as binary.

Large grid values create rhythmic loops, while small values create sonic artifacts. The No Triplets button sets grid division as binary.

blocks.text: Grid size can be changed randomly using the Variation control. If Variation is set to ”0”, grid size is fixed. But when Variation is set to higher values, the grid fluctuates considerably around the set Grid value. Variation has several different modes, available in the chooser below: Trigger creates variations of the grid when repetitions are triggered; 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16 trigger variations in regular intervals; and Auto forces Beat Repeat to apply a new random variation after each repetition — the most complex form of grid variation in Beat Repeat (especially if triplets are also allowed).

blocks.text: Beat Repeat’s repetitions can be pitched down for special sonic effects. Pitch is adjusted through resampling in Beat Repeat, lengthening segments to pitch them down without again compressing them to adjust for the length change. This means that the rhythmical structure can become quite ambiguous with higher Pitch values. The Pitch Decay control tapers the pitch curve, making each repeated slice play lower than the previous one. Warning: This is the most obscure parameter of Beat Repeat.

blocks.text: Beat Repeat includes a combined low-pass and high-pass filter for defining the passed frequency range of the device. You can turn the filter on and off, and set the center frequency and width of the passed frequency band, using the respective controls.

blocks.text: The original signal (which was received at Beat Repeat’s input) is mixed with Beat Repeat’s repetitions according to one of three mix modes: Mix allows the original signal to pass through the device and have repetitions added to it; Insert mutes the original signal when repetitions are playing but passes it otherwise; and Gate passes only the repetitions, never passing the original signal. Gate mode is especially useful when the effect is housed in a return track.

blocks.text: 29.8 Chorus-Ensemble
blocks.raw_html: 29.8 Chorus-Ensemble

blocks.text: Chorus-Ensemble offers a classic two-delay line chorus with an optional third delay line mode. It can produce a wide range of effects, from subtle thickening, through flanging and vibrato, to string ensemble chorus sounds.
blocks.raw_html: Chorus-Ensemble offers a classic two-delay line chorus with an optional third delay line mode. It can produce a wide range of effects, from subtle thickening, through flanging and vibrato, to string ensemble chorus sounds.

blocks.text: The device’s display shows the active delay lines as waveforms which reflect the currently selected effect mode and settings. Click one of the three buttons in the display to set the device to one of the available modes: Chorus, Ensemble, or Vibrato.
blocks.raw_html: The device’s display shows the active delay lines as waveforms which reflect the currently selected effect mode and settings. Click one of the three buttons in the display to set the device to one of the available modes: Chorus, Ensemble, or Vibrato.

blocks.text: Chorus mode creates a thickened sound by adding two time-modulated delayed signals to the input. Use it to achieve a classic chorus sound that adds light motion to your audio signal.
blocks.raw_html: Chorus mode creates a thickened sound by adding two time-modulated delayed signals to the input. Use it to achieve a classic chorus sound that adds light motion to your audio signal.

blocks.text: Ensemble mode is inspired by a thick three-delay line chorus pedal used in the ‘70s. It is based on and shares controls with Chorus mode, but creates a richer, smoother, and more intense chorus sound by using three delayed signals with evenly split modulation phase offsets.
blocks.raw_html: Ensemble mode is inspired by a thick three-delay line chorus pedal used in the ‘70s. It is based on and shares controls with Chorus mode, but creates a richer, smoother, and more intense chorus sound by using three delayed signals with evenly split modulation phase offsets.

blocks.text: Vibrato mode modulates the signal’s pitch to a greater extent than the Chorus and Ensemble modes, without layering it with a delayed signal. This produces a pronounced pitch variation rather than the thickening effect of the other modes. The shape of the modulation waveform can morph seamlessly from a sine to a triangle and can be used to create the classic “police siren” sound.

This produces a pronounced pitch variation rather than the thickening effect of the other modes. The shape of the modulation waveform can morph seamlessly from a sine to a triangle and can be used to create the classic “police siren” sound.

blocks.text: Each mode includes the option to enable a high-pass filter. When enabled, the filter reduces the modulation effect on signal components below the frequency set by the High-Pass Frequency slider, ranging from 20.0 Hz to 2.00 kHz.
blocks.raw_html: Each mode includes the option to enable a high-pass filter. When enabled, the filter reduces the modulation effect on signal components below the frequency set by the High-Pass Frequency slider, ranging from 20.0 Hz to 2.00 kHz.

blocks.text: In addition to the high-pass filter, the Chorus and Ensemble modes include the Width parameter, which sets the stereo width of the wet signal. This in turn adjusts the chorus level balance between the mid and side channels. At 0.0% the signal will be mono, at 100% the balance is equal, and at 200% the chorus level is twice as loud in the sides as in the middle. Width is used for maintaining the level of the effect across the stereo field, which can be helpful during mixing.

Width is used for maintaining the level of the effect across the stereo field, which can be helpful during mixing.

blocks.text: Chorus mode includes two additional parameters: Delay Time and Tap Count. The Delay Time chooser gives you the option to set a dynamic or fixed delay. When set to Auto, the delay time is scaled per tap and is directly proportional to the amount of modulation applied. When set to a fixed value, the delay time remains constant rather than scaling with the modulation amount. This makes it easier to produce a stable chorus effect without unwanted phasing or pitch modulation, which can be especially useful for bass or guitar sounds. Use the Taps toggles to switch between one- or two-tap delay. The single tap delay can help achieve simpler, broader chorus textures similar to classic hardware pedals.

blocks.text: Vibrato mode comes with Offset and Shape controls. Offset adjusts the amount of phase offset between the waveforms for the left and right channel. At 180°, the channels will be perfectly out of phase. Use Shape to change the shape of the modulation waveform. At 0.0%, the shape is set to a sine wave, while at 100%, the shape is set to a triangle wave.

blocks.text: Rate sets the modulation rate in Hertz, and can be adjusted either with the dial or by dragging up or down in the display. Turn up Rate for a more drastic chorus sound, or keep it low for more gentle phasing.

blocks.text: Amount adjusts the amplitude of the modulation signals that affects delay times. Higher values result in a stronger time deviation from the unmodulated time setting.

blocks.text: Feedback sets the amount of each channel’s output that is fed back to its input. Increasing this sounds more extreme and tends to increase upper harmonic material, and will also create audible delays if playback is stopped. The feedback signal can be inverted using the Feedback Invert toggle, enabling which results in a “hollow” sound when combined with high feedback values. Note that this control is disabled in Vibrato mode.

blocks.text: 29.8.1 Chorus-Ensemble Tips
blocks.raw_html: 29.8.1 Chorus-Ensemble Tips

blocks.text: Here are some tips for using Chorus-Ensemble: - Use Ensemble mode at a rate between 1 Hz and 1.8 Hz and 100% Amount on dry guitars to create a typical surf-rock sound. - Automate the Feedback Invert toggle at Feedback levels > 90% to create massive bursts of decaying oscillations.

blocks.text: 29.25 Looper
blocks.raw_html: 29.25 Looper

blocks.text: Looper is an audio effect based on classic real-time looping devices. It allows you to record and loop audio, creating endless overdubs that are synced to your Set. If the Set is not playing, Looper can analyze incoming audio and set Live’s tempo to match it. You can also predefine a loop length before recording and Live’s tempo will adjust so that your loop fits into the specified number of bars. Furthermore, audio can be imported to Looper to create a background for newly overdubbed material, or exported from Looper as a new clip.
blocks.raw_html: Looper is an audio effect based on classic real-time looping devices. It allows you to record and loop audio, creating endless overdubs that are synced to your Set. If the Set is not playing, Looper can analyze incoming audio and set Live’s tempo to match it. You can also predefine a loop length before recording and Live’s tempo will adjust so that your loop fits into the specified number of bars. Furthermore, audio can be imported to Looper to create a background for newly overdubbed material, or exported from Looper as a new clip.

blocks.text: The top half of Looper’s interface is a large display area optimized for easy readability during performance. During recording, the entire display area turns red. After recording, the display shows the current position in the loop and the total loop length in bars and beats.
blocks.raw_html: The top half of Looper’s interface is a large display area optimized for easy readability during performance. During recording, the entire display area turns red. After recording, the display shows the current position in the loop and the total loop length in bars and beats.

blocks.text: Looper’s transport buttons work in a similar way to other transport controls in Live. The Record button records incoming audio until another button is pressed. This overwrites any audio currently stored in Looper. Overdub continues to add additional layers of incoming audio that are the length of the originally recorded material. The Play button plays back the current state of Looper’s buffer without recording any new material. The Stop button stops playback.

This overwrites any audio currently stored in Looper. Overdub continues to add additional layers of incoming audio that are the length of the originally recorded material. The Play button plays back the current state of Looper’s buffer without recording any new material. The Stop button stops playback.

blocks.text: The behavior of the transport controls changes depending on whether or not Live’s playback is running. With the transport running, Looper behaves like a clip, and is subject to launch quantization as determined by the Quantization chooser. When Live’s playback is stopped, Looper’s transport engages immediately, regardless of the Quantization setting.

When Live’s playback is stopped, Looper’s transport engages immediately, regardless of the Quantization setting.

blocks.text: The Clear button erases Looper’s buffer. If you press Clear in Overdub mode while the transport is running, the contents of the buffer are cleared but the tempo and length are maintained. Pressing Clear in any other mode resets the tempo and length.

blocks.text: The Undo button erases everything that you’ve overdubbed since the last time Overdub was enabled. Your original recording, and anything that was overdubbed in a previous pass, is preserved. After pressing Undo, the button changes to Redo, which replaces the material removed by the last undo.

blocks.text: The large button below the transport controls is the Multi-Purpose Transport Button. As with the normal transport buttons, this button’s behavior changes depending on Looper’s current playback state, and whether or not material has already been recorded. If the buffer is empty, a single click starts recording. If Looper is recording, overdubbing or stopped, a single click switches to play mode. During playback, a click switches to overdub mode, allowing you to toggle back and forth between overdub and playback via additional single clicks.

blocks.text: Quickly pressing the button twice stops Looper, from either play or overdub mode. Clicking and holding the button for two seconds while in play mode activates Undo or Redo. Pressing and holding for two seconds while stopped clears Looper’s buffer.

blocks.text: Looper’s Multi-Purpose Transport Button is optimized for use with a MIDI footswitch. To assign a footswitch, enter MIDI Map Mode, click the button and then press your attached footswitch. Then exit MIDI Map Mode.

blocks.text: The Tempo Control chooser affects how Looper determines the tempo of recorded material:

blocks.text: None: Looper’s internal tempo is independent of Live’s global tempo.

blocks.text: Follow song tempo: The speed of Looper’s playback will be adjusted so that the recorded material plays back at Live’s global tempo.

blocks.text: Set & Follow song tempo: Live’s global tempo will be adjusted to match the tempo of material recorded into Looper. Any subsequent changes to Live’s global tempo will adjust the speed of Looper’s playback so that the recorded material plays back at the new global tempo.

blocks.text: The Record Length chooser is used to set the length of recorded material. Its behavior changes depending on whether or not Live’s global transport is running and, depending on the setting of the Tempo Control chooser, can set Live’s global tempo:

blocks.text: Song running: If Looper’s Record Length chooser is set to the default ”x bars,” Looper will record until you press another transport button. If you specify a fixed number of bars to record by selecting another option in the chooser, Looper will record for the specified time and then switch to Play or Overdub, as determined by the button next to this chooser.

blocks.text: Song not running: If Looper’s Record Length chooser is set to the default ”x bars,” Looper will make a guess about the tempo of the material you’ve recorded as soon as you press Overdub, Play or Stop. But this might result in a tempo that’s twice or half as fast as you’d like. If you first specify a fixed number of bars, Looper’s tempo will adjust so that your recording fits into this time.

blocks.text: The ”×2” button doubles the length of Looper’s recording buffer. Any material that you’ve already recorded will simply be duplicated. This allows you to, for example, record a series of one-bar ideas, and then overlay a series of two-bar ideas. The length and tempo of Looper’s buffer is shown in the display area.

blocks.text: The ”Drag me!” area in the display allows you to export Looper’s buffer as a new audio file. You can drag and drop to the browser or directly to a track, creating a new clip. The newly created clip’s Warp Mode will be set to Re-Pitch by default. You can also drag audio files to the ”Drag me!” area, which will replace the contents of Looper’s buffer. You can then use this material as a bed for further overdubs, for example.

blocks.text: Enabling the Reverse button plays the previously recorded material backwards. Any material that you overdub after enabling Reverse will be played forward. Note that disabling Reverse will then swap this behavior; the original material will play forward again, while the material that was overdubbed while Reverse was enabled will play backwards. Engaging the Reverse button is subject to the Quantization chooser setting.

Engaging the Reverse button is subject to the Quantization chooser setting.

blocks.text: Feedback sets the amount of previously recorded signal that is fed back into Looper when overdubbing. When set to 100%, the previously recorded material will never decrease in volume. When set to 50%, it will be half as loud with each repetition. Any changes to the Feedback amount won’t take effect until the next repetition. Note that Feedback has no effect in Play mode; each repetition will be at the same volume.

This is useful for situations in which you are feeding audio to multiple tracks, each containing its own Looper. If each of these Loopers is controlled with its own foot pedal, you can switch the recording and playback state while playing an instrument, without having to worry about monitor settings.

blocks.text: 29.29 Phaser-Flanger
blocks.raw_html: 29.29 Phaser-Flanger

blocks.text: Phaser-Flanger combines the functionalities of flanger and phaser effects into one device with separate modes, and offers an additional Doubler mode. All modes can be used to create lush, expressive sounds with a wide variety of tools and detailed options. Two LFOs and an envelope follower provide plenty of modulation possibilities.

blocks.text: You can choose between the three modes in the display:

blocks.text: Phaser, with its wide range of frequency and modulation ranges, creates wandering notch filters by feeding a phase-shifted version of the input signal back into the input. The phase shifting is achieved using modulated all-pass filters and has a lush sound.

blocks.text: Flanger creates a continuously changing comb filter effect by adding a time-modulated delayed signal with feedback to the input.
blocks.raw_html: • Flanger creates a continuously changing comb filter effect by adding a time-modulated delayed signal with feedback to the input.

blocks.text: Doubler creates the effect of doubled tracks (multiple stacked versions of similar recording takes) by adding time-modulated delayed signals to the input.

blocks.text: The display contains a visualization and the mode selector buttons. The visualization presents different information depending on the mode you choose and the LFO Stereo Mode’s settings (described in more detail below).

blocks.text: Notches increases or decreases the number of all-pass filters being used. Center chooses the center frequency of the notches. Spread increases or decreases the distance between the notches by adjusting the Q factor of the all-pass filters. Blend mixes the modulation routing between Center Frequency and Spread, with Center Frequency at 0.0 and Spread at 1.0.

blocks.text: In Flanger mode, the visualization shows how the modulation signal is affecting the delay time, with the left-most position equaling the value chosen in the Time parameter. blocks.text: Feedback sets the amount of each channel’s output that is fed back to its input. Increasing this sounds more extreme and tends to create a strong comb filtering effect, amplifying some frequencies and attenuating others. In Doubler Mode, it will also create audible delays if playback is stopped. The feedback signal can be inverted using the Ø button, which results in a “hollow” sound when combined with high feedback values.

blocks.text: 29.35 Shifter
blocks.raw_html: 29.35 Shifter

blocks.text: Shifter is a multi-purpose pitch and frequency-shifting audio effect that can be used to add ring modulation to incoming audio or to shift the pitch or frequency of audio in real time.

blocks.text: 29.35.1 Tuning and Delay Section
blocks.raw_html: 29.35.1 Tuning and Delay Section

blocks.text: The Coarse and Fine knobs adjust the pitch or frequency in the given value, depending on which shift mode (explained in the Shifter Mode section) is selected.

blocks.text: Enabling the Wide button inverts the polarity of the Spread value for the right channel, creating a stereo effect. This means that increasing the Spread value will shift the frequency down in the right channel while shifting it up in the left. Note that Wide has no effect if the Spread value is set to 0.

blocks.text: In Pitch mode, the Window slider adjusts the window size used by the algorithm. Low frequency signals often sound best with longer window sizes, while high frequencies often sound best with shorter window sizes. Tone cuts the high frequencies of the delay’s feedback path.

blocks.text: 29.35.6 Shifter Tips

blocks.text: 29.35.6.1 Pitch-shifted Drum Layers
blocks.raw_html: 29.35.6.1 Pitch-shifted Drum Layers

blocks.text: To add glitchy, metallic echoes to a drum loop, duplicate your drum track and add Shifter after the Drum Rack. In Pitch mode, try adjusting or automating the Coarse knob and enable the Delay button. Higher pitch shifts will create a metallic and crisp echoed delay. Lower pitch shifts will create a drawn-out delay effect. You can lower the volume of the pitch-shifted track so that it sits in the background, adding some movement to the main drum track.

blocks.text: In Ring mode, frequencies below the audible range (about 20 Hz or slightly lower) create a tremolo effect. You can also impart a sense of stereo motion to the tremolo by turning on Wide and using small Spread values.

blocks.text: 29.36 Spectral Resonator
blocks.raw_html: 29.36 Spectral Resonator

blocks.text: Spectral Resonator transforms an audio signal by applying tuned resonances to its spectrum. You can highlight chosen frequencies of the resonating partials and alter their decay, creating either short percussive reverberations or long washed-out tones. Choose which frequencies are affected through an internal resonator or via an external MIDI sidechain. Similar to a vocoder, you can use the MIDI input to place the resonances in key with its surrounding musical elements, playing the effect polyphonically with up to 16 voices. You can shape the signal further with different modulation modes to add movement and depth or create more fragmented, textural results. The effect also supports scale awareness and tuning systems.

blocks.text: 29.36.1 Pitch Mode Section
blocks.raw_html: 29.36.1 Pitch Mode Section

blocks.text: Spectral Resonator offers two modes that determine how the fundamental pitch of the effect’s resonant harmonics is set: Internal or MIDI.
blocks.raw_html: Spectral Resonator offers two modes that determine how the fundamental pitch of the effect’s resonant harmonics is set: Internal or MIDI.

blocks.text: When the Internal mode is enabled, the device is fixed to a single pitch, while in the MIDI mode the resonator is tuned dynamically according to external note input. Additional controls become available when MIDI mode is enabled:
blocks.raw_html: When the Internal mode is enabled, the device is fixed to a single pitch, while in the MIDI mode the resonator is tuned dynamically according to external note input. Additional controls become available when MIDI mode is enabled:

blocks.text: External Source and Tapping Point let you select any MIDI track as the input source and choose whether the signal is taken before or after MIDI effects in the track’s device chain. To use an external MIDI controller, select it in the Input Type chooser on a MIDI track, then select that track in Spectral Resonator’s External Source chooser.
blocks.raw_html: • External Source and Tapping Point let you select any MIDI track as the input source and choose whether the signal is taken before or after MIDI effects in the track’s device chain. To use an external MIDI controller, select it in the Input Type chooser on a MIDI track, then select that track in Spectral Resonator’s External Source chooser.

blocks.text: The Mono/Poly toggle switches between single and polyphonic voice modes. When set to Poly, Spectral Resonator can receive polyphonic material such as chords.
blocks.raw_html: • The Mono/Poly toggle switches between single and polyphonic voice modes. When set to Poly, Spectral Resonator can receive polyphonic material such as chords.

blocks.text: The Polyphony slider sets the number of voices the effect uses, from 2 to 16.
blocks.raw_html: • The Polyphony slider sets the number of voices the effect uses, from 2 to 16.

blocks.text: The MIDI Gate toggle determines how the resonator is activated. When set to On, the device functions more like an instrument and will only resonate only while MIDI notes are played. When set to Off, the resonator still responds to audio input, even without incoming notes. Note that MIDI Gate is always active in Poly mode.
blocks.raw_html: • The MIDI Gate toggle determines how the resonator is activated. When set to On, the device functions more like an instrument and will only resonate only while MIDI notes are played. When set to Off, the resonator still responds to audio input, even without incoming notes. Note that MIDI Gate is always active in Poly mode.

blocks.text: Glide adjusts the time it takes for pitch to slide between consecutive notes, in milliseconds. Note that the parameter is only active in Mono mode.
blocks.raw_html: • Glide adjusts the time it takes for pitch to slide between consecutive notes, in milliseconds. Note that the parameter is only active in Mono mode.

blocks.text: PB sets how much MIDI pitch bend messages shift the resonator’s pitch, from 0-24 semitones. Note that Spectral Resonator is also able to receive MPE data.
blocks.raw_html: • PB sets how much MIDI pitch bend messages shift the resonator’s pitch, from 0-24 semitones. Note that Spectral Resonator is also able to receive MPE data.

blocks.text: 29.36.2 Frequency Section
blocks.raw_html: 29.36.2 Frequency Section

blocks.text: When the Internal pitch mode is enabled, Spectral Resonator is tuned to the frequency set by the Freq control. You can adjust the frequency in Hertz or set it to a specific pitch; to toggle between the two options, use the Frequency Control Mode buttons below the Freq control. If the Use Current Scale toggle is on, the device follows the active clip scale instead. The control becomes SD Shift and can be used to transpose the resonator in scale degrees. Note that if scale awareness is enabled but no scale is active, Spectral Resonator follows the chromatic scale.
blocks.raw_html: When the Internal pitch mode is enabled, Spectral Resonator is tuned to the frequency set by the Freq control. You can adjust the frequency in Hertz or set it to a specific pitch; to toggle between the two options, use the Frequency Control Mode buttons below the Freq control. If the Use Current Scale toggle is on, the device follows the active clip scale instead. The control becomes SD Shift and can be used to transpose the resonator in scale degrees. Note that if scale awareness is enabled but no scale is active, Spectral Resonator follows the chromatic scale.

blocks.text: When the MIDI mode is enabled, Spectral Resonator is tuned to the frequencies of incoming MIDI notes. The MIDI input can be transposed by ±48 semitones using the Transp. control or by ±28 scale degrees when Use Current Scale is on. When the effect is scale aware, Transp. becomes the SD Shift control.
blocks.raw_html: When the MIDI mode is enabled, Spectral Resonator is tuned to the frequencies of incoming MIDI notes. The MIDI input can be transposed by ±48 semitones using the Transp. control or by ±28 scale degrees when Use Current Scale is on. When the effect is scale aware, Transp. becomes the SD Shift control.

blocks.text: Spectral Resonator works with tuning systems in both modes. When a tuning system is active, the Freq control in Internal mode and Transp. control in MIDI mode use note indices instead of note names and semitones, respectively.
blocks.raw_html: Spectral Resonator works with tuning systems in both modes. When a tuning system is active, the Freq control in Internal mode and Transp. control in MIDI mode use note indices instead of note names and semitones, respectively.

blocks.text: You can use the Stretch slider to adjust the spacing between the resonant harmonics. Values below 0% compress the distance, while values above 0 expand it. At 100%, only odd harmonics are produced, which leads to a square-wave type sound.
blocks.raw_html: You can use the Stretch slider to adjust the spacing between the resonant harmonics. Values below 0% compress the distance, while values above 0 expand it. At 100%, only odd harmonics are produced, which leads to a square-wave type sound.

blocks.text: The Shift slider transposes the spectrum of the input signal by ±48 semitones. Note that this affects the signal fed into the device and not the resonator’s own spectrum.
blocks.raw_html: The Shift slider transposes the spectrum of the input signal by ±48 semitones. Note that this affects the signal fed into the device and not the resonator’s own spectrum.

blocks.text: The Decay control sets how long the resonances persist. Higher values produce longer, sustained tones.
blocks.raw_html: The Decay control sets how long the resonances persist. Higher values produce longer, sustained tones.

blocks.text: HF Damp sets the amount of damping applied to high-frequency partials, while LF Damp sets the amount of damping applied to low-frequency partials. In both cases, the affected frequency ranges shift according to the current pitch (when in Internal mode) or the pitch of the incoming MIDI notes (when in MIDI mode).
blocks.raw_html: HF Damp sets the amount of damping applied to high-frequency partials, while LF Damp sets the amount of damping applied to low-frequency partials. In both cases, the affected frequency ranges shift according to the current pitch (when in Internal mode) or the pitch of the incoming MIDI notes (when in MIDI mode).

blocks.text: 29.36.3 Modulation Section
blocks.raw_html: 29.36.3 Modulation Section

blocks.text: You can set the effect to one of four modulation modes using the respective toggles: None, Chorus, Wander, or Granular. These modes determine how each harmonic’s pitch and amplitude are modulated:
blocks.raw_html: You can set the effect to one of four modulation modes using the respective toggles: None, Chorus, Wander, or Granular. These modes determine how each harmonic’s pitch and amplitude are modulated:

blocks.text: None applies no modulation.
blocks.raw_html: • None applies no modulation.

blocks.text: Chorus applies triangle wave modulation to each partial. When Mod Rate is set to 0, this mode only modulates the amplitudes of the partials.
blocks.raw_html: • Chorus applies triangle wave modulation to each partial. When Mod Rate is set to 0, this mode only modulates the amplitudes of the partials.

blocks.text: Wander uses random sawtooth waveforms as the modulation source for each partial.
blocks.raw_html: • Wander uses random sawtooth waveforms as the modulation source for each partial.

blocks.text: Granular modulates the amplitude of all partials randomly, using exponential decay envelopes. Partials are generated at irregular intervals, and the Mod Rate parameter affects their density.
blocks.raw_html: • Granular modulates the amplitude of all partials randomly, using exponential decay envelopes. Partials are generated at irregular intervals, and the Mod Rate parameter affects their density.

blocks.text: All modulation modes are also affected by the Mod Rate and Pch. Mod controls. Mod Rate sets the modulation rate, while Pch. Mod adjusts the range of pitch modulation in semitones. Although Pch. Mod displays only a positive value, pitch modulation is bipolar in all modes except Granular, where the grain envelopes are only applied in a positive direction.

blocks.text: 29.36.4 Spectrogram
blocks.raw_html: 29.36.4 Spectrogram

blocks.text: Spectral Resonator includes a spectrogram that displays the activity of frequencies in the dry and wet signals over time. Dry signals are shown in yellow and wet signals in blue. You can hide the spectrogram using the toggle in the upper-left corner of the display. The visualization helps identify which regions of the spectrum are being emphasized or modified by the resonator.
blocks.raw_html: Spectral Resonator includes a spectrogram that displays the activity of frequencies in the dry and wet signals over time. Dry signals are shown in yellow and wet signals in blue. You can hide the spectrogram using the toggle in the upper-left corner of the display. The visualization helps identify which regions of the spectrum are being emphasized or modified by the resonator.

blocks.text: Two controls are integrated into the spectrogram display: Harmonics and Quantize. You can use Harmonics to set the number of resonant harmonics used by the device. Higher values create a brighter sound, while lower values produce a darker timbre. Note that when using polyphony, the number of harmonics is evenly distributed between the voices, resulting in fewer harmonics per voice when high voice counts are used. Increasing harmonics also increases CPU usage.

Higher values create a brighter sound, while lower values produce a darker timbre. Increasing harmonics also increases CPU usage.

blocks.text: When Quantize is enabled, each harmonic is quantized to the active scale or tuning system. If no scale or tuning system is active, the harmonics are quantized to chromatic pitches instead.
blocks.raw_html: When Quantize is enabled, each harmonic is quantized to the active scale or tuning system. If no scale or tuning system is active, the harmonics are quantized to chromatic pitches instead.

blocks.text: 29.36.5 Global Parameters
blocks.raw_html: 29.36.5 Global Parameters

blocks.text: The Input Send control sets the amount of gain applied to the processed signal. A built-in limiter prevents the signal from clipping. The LED next to Input Send will light up when the limiter is in use.
blocks.raw_html: The Input Send control sets the amount of gain applied to the processed signal. A built-in limiter prevents the signal from clipping. The LED next to Input Send will light up when the limiter is in use.

blocks.text: The Unison parameter sets the number of unison voices, which are detuned copies of the resonator’s partials. Use the Uni. Amt parameter to adjust the amount of detuning between those voices. Increasing the number of voices thickens the sound, while higher detuning values create a wider and more animated character. In the Wander and Granular modulation modes, each voice is modulated independently, creating especially dense and warbly textures.

blocks.text: The Dry/Wet control adjusts the balance between the processed and unprocessed signals, and affects how prominently each signal appears in the spectrogram. Set Dry/Wet to 100% when using Spectral Resonator in a return track.

blocks.text: 29.36.6 Spectral Resonator Tips
blocks.raw_html: 29.36.6 Spectral Resonator Tips

blocks.text: Here are some ways you can use Spectral Resonator in your projects:
blocks.raw_html: Here are some ways you can use Spectral Resonator in your projects:

blocks.text: Create tonal drum loops by placing Spectral Resonator on a drum track and using the MIDI sidechain input to drive specific pitches. This can be used to add rhythm to your track, allowing the drum material to align tonally with other elements such as the bassline.
blocks.raw_html: • Create tonal drum loops by placing Spectral Resonator on a drum track and using the MIDI sidechain input to drive specific pitches. This can be used to add rhythm to your track, allowing the drum material to align tonally with other elements such as the bassline.

blocks.text: Set up Spectral Resonator to follow melodic pitches by first converting audio to MIDI with Convert Harmony to New MIDI Track or Convert Melody to New MIDI Track, then routing the generated MIDI track into the effect.
blocks.raw_html: • Set up Spectral Resonator to follow melodic pitches by first converting audio to MIDI with Convert Harmony to New MIDI Track or Convert Melody to New MIDI Track, then routing the generated MIDI track into the effect.

blocks.text: Create reverb-like sounds by setting Freq to a low value, increasing Unison and Uni. Amt values, and using the Wander modulation mode in combination with low Mod Rate and Pch. Mod values. Adjust the Decay parameter to control the “reverb” decay.
blocks.raw_html: • Create reverb-like sounds by setting Freq to a low value, increasing Unison and Uni. Amt values, and using the Wander modulation mode in combination with low Mod Rate and Pch. Mod values. Adjust the Decay parameter to control the “reverb” decay.

blocks.text: Use Spectral Resonator like a vocoder by placing the effect on a vocal track and controlling it via MIDI sidechain input.
blocks.raw_html: • Use Spectral Resonator like a vocoder by placing the effect on a vocal track and controlling it via MIDI sidechain input.

blocks.text: Layer harmonics by placing two Spectral Resonators in series and sending different MIDI signals to each one to create overlapping resonant structures.
blocks.raw_html: • Layer harmonics by placing two Spectral Resonators in series and sending different MIDI signals to each one to create overlapping resonant structures.

blocks.text: 29.37 Spectral Time
blocks.raw_html: 29.37 Spectral Time

blocks.text: Spectral Time combines time freezing and spectral delay effects in a single inspiring device. You can resynthesize your sounds by applying various spectral filters, delays and frequency-shifting techniques to incoming material, creating highly varied and unique copies. The freeze and delay effects can be used together or independently, allowing for a wide range of possibilities, such as sustaining any sound infinitely, or combining delays with time-synced fade transitions. You can easily transform sounds by smearing frequencies over time, or add metallic echoes and space to any sound source.
blocks.raw_html: Spectral Time combines time freezing and spectral delay effects in a single inspiring device. You can resynthesize your sounds by applying various spectral filters, delays and frequency-shifting techniques to incoming material, creating highly varied and unique copies. The freeze and delay effects can be used together or independently, allowing for a wide range of possibilities, such as sustaining any sound infinitely, or combining delays with time-synced fade transitions. You can easily transform sounds by smearing frequencies over time, or add metallic echoes and space to any sound source.

blocks.text: Spectral Time has two main sections, Freezer and Delay, which can be used individually or serially, with the freezer feeding the delay. You can toggle the individual sections using the Freezer On and Delay On buttons.
blocks.raw_html: Spectral Time has two main sections, Freezer and Delay, which can be used individually or serially, with the freezer feeding the delay. You can toggle the individual sections using the Freezer On and Delay On buttons.

blocks.text: Spectral Time uses a spectrogram to display how frequencies in the dry and wet signals behave over time. Dry signals are represented in yellow, while wet signals are shown in blue. You can hide the visualization by clicking on its toggle button.
blocks.raw_html: Spectral Time uses a spectrogram to display how frequencies in the dry and wet signals behave over time. Dry signals are represented in yellow, while wet signals are shown in blue. You can hide the visualization by clicking on its toggle button.

blocks.text: From Spectral Time’s context menu, you can switch Zero Dry Signal Latency on or off. Enabling it reduces the latency of the dry signal to zero instead of syncing it with the output of the effect. This option is useful when playing a live instrument through Spectral Time and monitoring the output.

blocks.text: 29.37.1 Freezer Section
blocks.raw_html: 29.37.1 Freezer Section

blocks.text: Depending on which of the Manual/Retrigger Mode buttons are activated, the Freezer section controls how the freeze function is triggered and how certain temporal characteristics of the frozen audio are affected. Note that for both modes, the Freeze button also has to be toggled in order for the effect to occur.
blocks.raw_html: Depending on which of the Manual/Retrigger Mode buttons are activated, the Freezer section controls how the freeze function is triggered and how certain temporal characteristics of the frozen audio are affected. Note that for both modes, the Freeze button also has to be toggled in order for the effect to occur.

blocks.text: In Manual mode, audio can be frozen by clicking on the Freeze button. You can also control the Fade In and Fade Out time of the frozen signal in milliseconds.
blocks.raw_html: In Manual mode, audio can be frozen by clicking on the Freeze button. You can also control the Fade In and Fade Out time of the frozen signal in milliseconds.

blocks.text: In Retrigger mode, you have more controls to fine-tune the rhythm of the frozen audio, which can be frozen automatically at every transient (onset), or at regular intervals.
blocks.raw_html: In Retrigger mode, you have more controls to fine-tune the rhythm of the frozen audio, which can be frozen automatically at every transient (onset), or at regular intervals.

blocks.text: Onsets mode will freeze the audio after a transient is detected in the input. Use the Sensitivity knob to adjust the sensitivity of onset detection. Sensitivity is highest at 100% and lowest at 0%.
blocks.raw_html: Onsets mode will freeze the audio after a transient is detected in the input. Use the Sensitivity knob to adjust the sensitivity of onset detection. Sensitivity is highest at 100% and lowest at 0%.

blocks.text: Sync mode will freeze the audio at regular intervals, determined by the Interval control. By toggling the Freezer Time Unit buttons, the Interval control can be set to either milliseconds or beat-time values.
blocks.raw_html: Sync mode will freeze the audio at regular intervals, determined by the Interval control. By toggling the Freezer Time Unit buttons, the Interval control can be set to either milliseconds or beat-time values.

blocks.text: In both Onsets and Sync modes, the Freezer Fade Shape buttons toggle between two available fade shapes: Crossfade and Envelope. Both fade shapes have different controls to determine how a new freeze will fade in and out.
blocks.raw_html: In both Onsets and Sync modes, the Freezer Fade Shape buttons toggle between two available fade shapes: Crossfade and Envelope. Both fade shapes have different controls to determine how a new freeze will fade in and out.

blocks.text: When the Crossfade shape is selected, the new freeze will fade in and the old freeze (or dry signal) will fade out. The crossfade duration is set by the X-Fade control, which specifically determines the time in milliseconds over which a new freeze will fade in as a percentage of the sync interval set by the Interval control.

blocks.text: When the Envelope shape is selected, a new freeze will fade in and out according to the millisecond time values chosen in the Fade In and Fade Out parameters. In this mode, up to eight simultaneous freezes can be stacked on top of one another.

blocks.text: 29.42 Vocoder
blocks.raw_html: 29.42 Vocoder

blocks.text: (Note: The Vocoder effect is not available in the Intro and Lite Editions.)
blocks.raw_html: (Note: The Vocoder effect is not available in the Intro and Lite Editions.)

blocks.text: A vocoder is an effect that combines the frequency information of one audio signal (called the carrier) with the amplitude contour of another audio signal (called the modulator). The modulator source is generally something with a clear rhythmic character such as speech or drums, while the carrier is typically a harmonically-rich synthesizer sound such as a string or pad. The most familiar application of a vocoder is to create ”talking synthesizer” or robotic voice effects.
blocks.raw_html: A vocoder is an effect that combines the frequency information of one audio signal (called the carrier) with the amplitude contour of another audio signal (called the modulator). The modulator source is generally something with a clear rhythmic character such as speech or drums, while the carrier is typically a harmonically-rich synthesizer sound such as a string or pad. The most familiar application of a vocoder is to create ”talking synthesizer” or robotic voice effects.

blocks.text: Vocoders work by running both the carrier and modulator signals through banks of band-pass filters. The output level of each of the modulator’s filters is then analyzed and used to control the volume of the corresponding filter for the carrier signal.
blocks.raw_html: Vocoders work by running both the carrier and modulator signals through banks of band-pass filters. The output level of each of the modulator’s filters is then analyzed and used to control the volume of the corresponding filter for the carrier signal.

blocks.text: Live’s Vocoder should be inserted on the track that contains the audio material you plan to use as your modulator. The Carrier chooser then provides a variety of options for the carrier signal:
blocks.raw_html: Live’s Vocoder should be inserted on the track that contains the audio material you plan to use as your modulator. The Carrier chooser then provides a variety of options for the carrier signal:

blocks.text: Noise uses Vocoder’s internal noise generator as the carrier source. With this selected, an X-Y display is shown which allows you to adjust the character of the noise. The horizontal axis adjusts downsampling. Click and drag to the left to decrease the sample rate of the carrier’s output. The vertical axis adjusts the density of the noise. Click and drag downward to decrease the density.
blocks.raw_html: • Noise uses Vocoder’s internal noise generator as the carrier source. With this selected, an X-Y display is shown which allows you to adjust the character of the noise. The horizontal axis adjusts downsampling. Click and drag to the left to decrease the sample rate of the carrier’s output. The vertical axis adjusts the density of the noise. Click and drag downward to decrease the density.

blocks.text: External allows you to select any available internal routing points from the choosers below. This is the option you’ll want for classic ”robot voice” applications.
blocks.raw_html: • External allows you to select any available internal routing points from the choosers below. This is the option you’ll want for classic ”robot voice” applications.

blocks.text: Modulator uses the modulator itself as the carrier. This essentially outputs a resynthesized version of the modulator signal, but allows you to use Vocoder’s sound-shaping controls to adjust the sound.
blocks.raw_html: • Modulator uses the modulator itself as the carrier. This essentially outputs a resynthesized version of the modulator signal, but allows you to use Vocoder’s sound-shaping controls to adjust the sound.

blocks.text: Pitch Tracking enables a monophonic oscillator, which tunes itself to the pitch of the modulator. The High and Low sliders allow you to limit the frequency range that the oscillator will attempt to track. Choose from sawtooth or one of three pulse waveforms and adjust the coarse tuning of the oscillator via the Pitch slider. Pitch tracking is particularly effective with monophonic modulator sources such as melodic instruments or voices. Note that the oscillator only updates its frequency when it detects a clear pitch. It then maintains this pitch until it detects a new one. This means that changing the oscillator’s parameters or causing it to reset (when grouping Vocoder’s track, for example) can cause unexpected changes in the sound. With polyphonic material or drums, pitch tracking is generally unpredictable (but can be very interesting.)

Choose from sawtooth or one of three pulse waveforms and adjust the coarse tuning of the oscillator via the Pitch slider. Pitch tracking is particularly effective with monophonic modulator sources such as melodic instruments or voices. Note that the oscillator only updates its frequency when it detects a clear pitch. It then maintains this pitch until it detects a new one. This means that changing the oscillator’s parameters or causing it to reset (when grouping Vocoder’s track, for example) can cause unexpected changes in the sound. With polyphonic material or drums, pitch tracking is generally unpredictable (but can be very interesting.)

blocks.text: Particularly when using external carrier sources, a vocoder’s output can sometimes lose a lot of high end. Enabling the Enhance button results in a brighter sound by normalizing the spectrum and dynamics of the carrier.
